utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Selimi, if I would remind you of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence. That still applies. Thank you, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: We've had some very quick testimony, but not that quick.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Mr. Selimi, good afternoon. You will recall on Friday we had reached or just about to reach 1997 and then the return of Fatmir Limaj to Kosovo in 1998. So we're dealing with that period. And I'LL come straight to Fatmir Limaj himself. Do you recall where or when it was that you first met Fatmir Limaj upon his return to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Could you just kindly tell us what you recall about that.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the time when Fatmir Limaj returned from abroad was a time when many were coming back to Kosova. It was a time after 5th of March, 1998, after the heroic fall of legendary commander Adem Jashari and the mobilisation of people to support the KLA was of a high level. Amongst those who returned to Kosova to fight for its freedom was Fatmir Limaj. The time I met him was early March or mid-March 1998 in Likovc, Drenica area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And when you met him, was he on his own or with a group? What was the position?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall it in details, but I believe he was with other men who came either together, either separately, and who at the time were all gathering at Likovc.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Was there a particular reason why they were gathering there at Likovc?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course there was. Not only Likovc but entire Drenica was a zone where combat was going on between the KLA forces and the repressive forces of the Serb government, the Serb police forces. Drenica was an area where frontal combat was going on between the KLA forces and the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, at that time was that the only operational zone in Kosovo or were there other ones of an equal nature?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time it seems that this was the only zone where KLA soldiers gathered. It was the only of the kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, in relation to, therefore, Drenica zone in March of 1998, could you tell us a little about how that was organised, if it was organised at all.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The organisation of KLA soldiers at that time depended on the circumstances that occurred earlier. One of the biggest events that dictated the organisation was the end of 1997, the public appearance of the KLA, the beginning of 1998 when the massacres at Qirez and Likoshan took place, and the events of the 5th and 6th of March, the Jashari epic. So people were seeking possible forms in order to join the military forces and defend their country. And at that time it was an authentic military organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Can you just explain how it worked?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we look at it from a perspective, the KLA army had appeared on the scene for several years now, that it had a guerrilla structure not concentrated in many zones but its epicentre in Drenica. The KLA had started with its activities and tend and significance to create a military structure that would overtake the war for the liberation of Kosova. To this time, it was -- it resembled more of a horizontal structure and had one organ which was at that time called central staff. The number was limited.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, just two questions arising out of that answer. They may be related. You mentioned it had a guerrilla structure and then it resembled more of a horizontal structure. Are those two things the same or were you meaning to define two different things?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately. They are similar and can act together. Regardless of being horizontal or vertical, a structure cannot operate without an organ. In this context, I want to say that the KLA had created several guerrilla units scattered in designated zones of Kosova, but mainly in Drenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, can I go back to Fatmir Limaj. How long do you remember that he remained in Likovc?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I cannot say exactly how long it was, but it was a relatively short time until he was -- it was possible for him to move to somewhere else or to stay there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I want to deal with his moving to somewhere else. Do you know where he went when he left Likovc?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a practice which more or less was a rule. Those volunteers who joined the KLA would be best if they returned to their birthplace or to their native areas. This practice was applied in Fatmir's case as well, who at that time went to this -- to his native place in order to see what his role would be in organisation or in organising the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And which area was that that he was going to? Did you know where he was going?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fatmir Limaj was born in Banje, Malisheve municipality, and he went to the Malisheve region.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: After he left, did you keep in contact with him somehow?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, how was that done? How did you keep in contact with him?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he returned to Likovc once, or maybe I met him in Malisheve. However, we maintained contacts in order to discuss things and to see what we could do and to discuss his possibilities for being in the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And what did you discover on those occasions when you did meet him to discuss how things were going?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot call it a discovery, but in discussion with Fatmir, we assessed the situation, and regarding the zones in Malisheve, we thought we should find people, volunteers who will join the KLA and, if possible, to be in accordance with the circumstances in this region.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I know it's a rather obvious question, this next one, but had Fatmir Limaj been ordered to go to Malisevo in order to establish units if he could?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He couldn't have been ordered since still his position in the KLA was not defined.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, did there come a time later when his position became a little more defined, as you put?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And how much later? He's arrived back in March. You saw him in March and he's left. So how long after March was it that you, as it were, could say his position was a little more defined?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this could not have been done in a short time because those zones, those villages, didn't have any kind of pre-organisation. So it took relatively long for the KLA army to begin with the formation of the operative units in that part as well, which was later called a zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Can you perhaps give us some idea how long it took for that to happen?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we consider the circumstances that occurred at that time in Kosova, it was difficult to be done [as interpreted] that rapidly. So it took us almost the whole summer to begin with the formation of such a structure. It was end of summer when we started our attempts to organise an operational zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I'm sorry to ask you the detail if you can remember it, but what was the problems that you were facing in that period of time?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the main problems was the Serb offensives and attacks against us and against the population. This was the main problem that was an obstacle in us organising the structure of the KLA. Secondly, the infrastructure. This was another problem for us. The population had at that time fled to Drenica area and to less difficult areas like Malisheve. Another problem was that we lacked soldiers and volunteers to create a zone that we will -- we will later create. These were the main problems that we faced.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, during this time -- we started your evidence with you indicated that you were on the General Staff or central staff, however defined. What was your own position in these months, March, April, May of 1998?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until May 1998 when it was still a central staff of the KLA, there wasn't a definition of tasks, but all people who were in this staff were members of this staff without any specific definition of their duties and tasks. After May 1998 and after the restructuring of the Drenica staff, I became the operational chief of the KLA, a G3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And did that change at any time in 1998? Did you take on another role?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Approximately sometime in August I took up another task and that was of the general inspector of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And could you -- it may be self-evident, but could you just describe what you had to do as the general inspector of the KLA from August onwards.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In accordance with the appointment, it is obvious what is role of a general inspector is in a certain structure, but under the circumstances at that time was to follow the development and the formation of the operational units at that time who were in their initial phase of formation. So this was the role that at that time, to inspect how these units were being formed and to provide them with any necessary assistance that they required.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, just before dealing a little with that situation, you mentioned that Fatmir Limaj came to see you in Likovc. Did you go and see him at any time in Klecka or anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And again, just approximately. I'm dealing with March through to August period principally. How many -- roughly how many times do you think you may have visited him?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe you will excuse me for not being able to give you an exact figure. I forgot how many times, but I have been several times and not that rarely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And when you visited him, again I have to ask you this way around, what would be the purpose of your visit to him?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was more or less the same aim, to see what possibilities and ways we could use to spread out in other areas of Malisheve. Another reason was that I knew Fatmir from before. There were other reasons such as to find out the ways and the forms of calling on new volunteers to join the ranks of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I want to ask you the position with regard to weaponry in this period, particularly not in Drenica so many but where Fatmir Limaj was. What sort of weaponry was available that you remember?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general, but since you are asking me in particular about that area, the weaponry was composed of light infantry rifles of small calibres. If you want me to give details, then I may do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd just give a few examples of what you're speaking about.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say infantry rifles, I have in mind the most usual weapons like 7.62 and 7.9 calibre, and other weapons of more or less the same calibre which were usually hand-held weapons and infantry weapons with some minor exceptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And did you, upon these visits to see Fatmir Limaj, did you discover whether in fact he'd managed to form a unit or not?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since Fatmir was based in Klecka, he had been in a position to have around him a group of KLA fighters which was called Celiku 1. At least this is what I know it to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Did you know about any other groups that had taken on the name Celiku?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that region and at that time there were other units whose name was not Celiku only. There were other units like Pellumbi, Lumi, Hekuri, and other similar units. But there were also other Celiku units to my recollection, like Celiku 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5. I apologise for not giving you the exact number of Celiku units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, so far as Fatmir Limaj was concerned and only as far as you knew, what was the unit that he was associated with?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that question is very leading on an important topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: No, I agree [sic]. It isn't very leading. So I'm not -- I'm trying to avoid using words that are leading. So the question, I'll put it another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: What unit or units had any connection to Fatmir Limaj?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The units that had connection to Fatmir Limaj was actually unit number 1. I may know this better because I have in mind a specific case for two minor reasons. It might be one of the first KLA groups that was formed in that region and because of the code they use in radio communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I want to ask you about the stage when a brigade was formed. Are you familiar with that stage?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, of course. Because in one way or another, I was involved in the formation of the operational units beginning from the operational units of Drenica operational zone, which had up to a time formed -- it might had been mid-summer it had formed four operational brigades or the nucleus of these brigades to pass on at a later phase to the creation of other zones such as the Pashtrik operational zone, which I can't tell you exactly how many brigades it had, but it started with Brigade 121.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I just want to ask you about Pashtrik zone. Who was in charge of the zone, Pashtrik zone, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person in charge of that zone -- we had two -- we had conceived of two phases in regard to the creation of that zone. The first phase was the phase of spreading the idea, and then this phase was not in conformity to what we did later, because initially we thought to have the Pashtrik zone in another area. But because of the changing circumstances, in August 1998 we deemed it appropriate that the Pashtrik operational zone be formed in the form that it got later, beginning from Brigade 121 to 127.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: You were, may I pause a moment, because I understand there are problems with interpretation. Right. I think it may be we both of us have to slow down a little for the interpreters. I'm not sure whether that's the right message.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, again a rather obvious question for you, but who became in charge of the 121 Brigade?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be in charge of a unit you have to be appointed. The commander of Brigade 121, following the formation of the Pashtrik operational zone and the formation of this brigade, was appointed Fatmir Limaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, I just want to move on a slight amount of time. We know after that, much later in the year, he also was appointed to the General Staff. Do you remember that stage? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And what do you recall his role was on the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially his role was not defined. His job description was not prepared. After he performed several tasks as a member, he became chief of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, between August -- do you remember when that was that he was on the General Staff, before I ask the next question?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think approximately after the formation of the Drenica operational zone, which was the first operational zone of the KLA. It must have been end of August or the beginning of September when Fatmir Limaj was appointed brigade -- commander of Brigade 121, which at that time was called Ismet Jashari Kumanova Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: How many operational zones were eventually created?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And can you just name, if you can remember them, the seven zones as you recall it?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Drenica operational zone, which is the first one to be created, which had four brigades. Brigade 111 to 114, then Pashtrik operational zone, the second operational zone created parallel with a Dukadjin zone, and it had Brigade 121 to 127 brigades. And respectively, the Dukadjin operational zone having brigade 131 to 138. Then the Shale operational zone as the fourth operational zone created, which had two brigades, 141 and 142 Brigade. And then the Llap operational zone, which likewise had three brigades beginning from Brigade 151 to 153. Then came the Nerodimlje operational zone, which had Brigade 161 to 162. And the last operational zone was the Karadak operational zone with Brigade 171, 172. But process of formation and structuring of the zones did not finish until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you for the details of all the various KLA members who were in charge of each of the zones, but do you remember them if somebody needs to ask you who they were?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: All right. Now, during this period again, this is a period from May, June, July, August, through August and the brigades, was the General Staff located in one place or not?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The General Staff was based in several places, and usually its members moved to -- from one zone to another.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: How long would it remain in any one place?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depended on the circumstances of the war and the need to be at a certain zone to assist the General Staff to form the zone or the respective units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Was it ever anywhere near Klecka as a location?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And where was that and when was that?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was located in Divjak village twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Do you remember when the two occasions were?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time it was before the outbreak of fighting, that is before the war, in the course of the formation of the guerrilla units. But it doesn't mean that it was the seat of the General Staff. It just utilised a facility, the house of a family in that area as its base. During 1997, it stopped using that use or that facility to use it again in 1998 initially very secretly and now and again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: On the second occasion when you used it now and again, how long would it remain there when it went, hours, days, weeks? How can we measure it?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depended. I might say that when it needed to hold meetings for several hours, then at the end of summer or in the summer of 1997 it was -- excuse me, 1998, it was based there in Divjak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, at that time how many -- that is, when it's based there at the end of the summer, how many people were on the General Staff besides yourself?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in that particular house or in general in the structure of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: In general.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The structure of the General Staff of the KLA varied, I mean the number of this structure, having new members joining it and the number of the departments established. So we cannot give you a fixed number to define the number of the members of the General Staff at that time, because the number increased, varied.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Perhaps I could ask you this, and if it's too difficult, please say so, but I'd like to deal with the beginning of August. If you could -- that is of 1998. Can you recollect how many members there were then and how many departments, as you put it, there were then?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until that time, we had established the most necessary departments but had not completed the structure of a usual General Staff in a regular army. We had focused our efforts on the establishment of the most necessary departments which might be functional in the circumstances beginning with the department which was very important at that time for us of taking evidence of all the materials we possessed at the time, the department of public information, the public -- the department of operations, and the department of logistics. These were some of the departments set up at that time as the most crucial in our view for the functioning of the General Staff under those circumstances. But the structure of the staff, as I said, changed depending on the developments and events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I want to ask you, as this case concerns the village of Lapusnik and its surrounding area, before the war had you ever been to Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had passed through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, could you be a little more explicit? In other words, just explain what you mean by you had passed through it.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know that Lapusnik is a village through which a road passes. It is an intercity road and, as such, thousands of people pass through Lapusnik in a day. There is an asphalt road that divides it. As such, many people have passed through this village, the village of Lapusnik, and I was one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Had you visited the village itself? In other words, got out of a vehicle, gone into a building or a house or whatever in the village?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, during these months we're dealing with, again April, May, June, July, August of 1998, did you go to the village as opposed to passing by on the main road? Did you go to the village in that period of time?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Usually I have passed by Lapusnik before the war, because it was a very important road, the road that ran through Lapusnik. During the war, it was also very important -- there was another road which was very important, too, and which also ran through Lapusnik. It was a road used by us as well as by the population. We passed from Drenica zone to the villages of Malisheve.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, if I showed you a map would you be able to point out the two roads you've been talking about?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I'm seeing if we've got a spare copy of one, but I don't think we have. Could we have, please, map 6 of P1. If there is a clean copy that would help, but if there isn't we'll just use the one that's in the Prosecution bundle. P1, 6. It doesn't matter. If the original Prosecution Exhibit is there, that will do. It's Exhibit 1. It's this folder. P1, map 6. There's one -- Mr. Whiting is holding one in his hand. That's it. P1, map 6. Yes, that's it. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And if it could be put on the monitor to your left-hand side so that you can then look at it. And if you have a pen or something you can point with, and then if you look at the map. You described two roads, and are the two roads on the map and, if so, can you point to the two roads and describe them as you point, please?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning, I would like to point out that I didn't say two main roads, but I just said two roads. The Peja-Pristina main road can be seen clearly here, and I can describe it. It begins at Fushe Kosove and then goes by Slatine, Korretice, Komorane, Lapusnik, and continues towards Orlat and in the direction of Peja. This is a main road in Kosova and links to big centres, Peja and Pristina. The other road that I mentioned and which came into use during the war, I cannot point it -- exactly where it is, but it's in this area and it links the villages of Drenica which were in the war zone at that time to the villages in Malisheve. It's 2 or 300 metres from Lapusnik gorge in the direction of Peja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to ask you just one or two more questions about Lapusnik. Whilst you were on the General Staff, did you hear of any prison camp in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about this when the indictment against Limaj, Bala, and Musliu was issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Had you heard about it in particular before that and obviously in 1998 itself?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Would you wait there, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Nor I, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I begin my cross-examination, I have -- there's a small procedural matter which I'd like to raise with the Court, and to do so I'd ask if the witness could be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be short, will it, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Selimi, would you be good enough to go with the court officer for a few moments. There's a procedural matter to be discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before Mr. Whiting begins, I waited for the witness to depart in case it is a different issue, but if it's the issue upon which we've had a little notice, it doesn't apply to this witness as I understand it, and therefore --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's not that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: It isn't that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm so glad.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is -- I would like to cross-examine this witness in part on the basis of an interview that the witness gave as part of a documentary which was broadcast on television. It is -- in our view this documentary has been disclosed insofar as it is included in the Electronic Disclosure Suite and therefore a search by the -- a search of the witnesses name in the Electronic Disclosure Suite would reveal this documentary. I also think that as it is a prior statement of the witness, an interview that the witness himself gave, there -- it is something he should be familiar with, should be aware of and should be able to deal with. However, because in issue arose in what I would suggest is a different form during the testimony of Mr. Limaj, I wanted to raise it just before the cross-examination started in case there was any difficulty about -- about disclosure or notice and, if so, how that would -- I'd like to give it -- I can make the Defence aware of it now. I think, in my view, it's a horse of a different colour from the issue -- well, I see the Judge shaking his head. Maybe that's the argument or the expression I've used, but I think it's something -- this is a different matter. This is, as I said, it's been disclosed. It is -- it is an interview of the witness himself. He should be familiar with it. I would expect the Defence could be familiar with it. In any event, I wanted to raise it to have it aired before the cross-examination started so that when it came to that we wouldn't have an interruption of that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So you give notice that you propose to cross-examine in part with respect to an interview given by this witness to --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's to the media; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And that it is in the general disclosure, electronic form, made by the OTP but it has not been specifically disclosed as a separate identified document, if I can call it that, to this Defence in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's correct. I think that's fair summary of the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Does any issue arise, Mr. Mansfield?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure, if I may put it that way at the moment, because firstly it's not been made clear to what purpose it is being used. In other words, is it being suggested it's a prior inconsistent statement, and at the moment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This is cross-examination of a Defence witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. So it's not entirely clear to what purpose it goes. Just because it's Defence witness doesn't mean that the Prosecution can cross-examine on absolutely anything. But more importantly, as far as disclosure's concerned, the problem here is, and I'm make it clear we don't have a transcript of this. I'm not suggesting it's not on the EDS system, it's just that that manner of disclosure does result in a mass of material being certainly able to be accessed with a certain amount of diligence, and it does mean in some cases quite a considerable amount of analysis to reach whatever it is that's going to be relied on. Certainly it's not a document in the normal course of events for which we have signed as we do on many occasions for particular interviews. So I don't know what's in this one. And if, in fact, there had been an intention to use this and we have notified obviously Prosecution well in advance of these witnesses, then we, we say, could have been highlighted by the Prosecution before now, because I'm not quite sure how we're supposed to deal with it when Mr. Whiting's had plenty of opportunity to let us know that that's what he intends to do with this document so we can address it in a more relevant way. At the moment I don't know what's on it and therefore I don't know for what purpose it's going to be used in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Since I have -- I have not been directly involved in the questioning of this witness, my remarks are necessarily a bit briefer than they would have been if I was. I have as an initial concern the question of whether or not to the extent this document has relevance whether it is from what I'm gathering potential impeachment on a collateral matter or not. I have no way of knowing of that initially. The second problem that I think this creates, which is a problem that has been raised in prior filing, is that the disclosure system as is set up on the EDS is a relatively vast system and at times it works and at other times it does not. At times we're able to in fact focus and make a determination that we have all the information that concerns any given witness. Sometimes we are not. Unfortunately, I can't speak to that issue directly and was just trying to double-check that as a matter of fact to make a determination whether or not our search of the EDS, which is relatively consistent search, is one which we've been able to identify this document and specifically identify this document as it relates to this particular witness. So I am in the same position that Mr. Mansfield is in with regard Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to the issue. I'm not particularly sure for what purposes the Prosecution is intending on using this information, and perhaps an offer of proof and a focused statement to the Chamber with regard to what the specific purpose is of the use of this document might be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I have nothing to add. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course the material in the EDS itself is vast, just like the material in the Prosecution's evidence system is vast. This material -- I would expect searches by names of witnesses to be routinely done. It would be disclosed. That's a much narrower category that would be discovered. We have not had this document in our possession for a long time. We did our own search, and this just came up at the end of last week and came to our possession. As a practical matter, I'm not sure -- I'm not sure I understand the -- a disclosure regime where the Prosecution would be required -- I mean -- let me back up for a moment. We -- we -- as the Court is well aware, we received a long list of witness names a few weeks ago. We have been scrambling and doing our best to learn as much as we can about these witnesses. Information comes in at the last minute. The -- we learn of witnesses that are going to testify a week or so ahead of time. So necessarily, our own research uncovers documents and information days before the witness testifies. I'm not sure I understand a disclosure regime where the Prosecution would be required to disclose its cross-examination before the witness testifies by showing all of -- everything that it's going to use including prior statements that are available both to the Defence by just inquiry of the witness and also through the EDS. Certainly that's not something that happened during the Prosecution case. We were not provided with the Defence -- the documents that the Defence was going to use in cross-examination even though we requested it. The Defence had in its possession interviews of our witnesses. We asked for them. We were not given them. And therefore, I don't understand why the rules would be different for us. I would suggest that cross-examination, we should have the opportunity to test the witness, and if we are required beforehand, days beforehand to provide a road map of our cross-examination, well, that necessarily would give the opportunity to the witness to think of answers to the questions and prepare beforehand, and that's necessarily in the interests of discovering the truth. And so I don't think that the Prosecution has done anything improper here. I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't think that's being suggested.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I think, then, the Prosecution should be allowed to use the document. I should also say -- I should also say that it's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I understand Mr. Mansfield and Mr. Guy-Smith to be saying it would be more practical. They would know whether they had any particular objection, and they would be prepared to follow your cross-examination if they knew that you were going to be dealing with a particular document rather than it being merely a document among perhaps very many in the electronic suite. I didn't understand it to get higher than that, on what was put by Mr. Mansfield and Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm happy to share the document now, and it will not necessarily arise in the cross-examination. It depends -- it depends on answers that are given by the witness to questions about activities that occurred before the war. And depending on his answers, it may or may not become necessary to put this document to him. But I'm happy to share the specific document with the Defence now so they're aware of it, and I think it will be clear to them where and how it might arise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I indicate from the Chamber's point of view that with cross-examination, whether it is by Defence of a Prosecution witness or vice versa, it has not been the practice, as it is not usually the practice in adversarial systems of which I am aware, for those cross-examining, as it were, to give notice of what they propose to do to the other side. There may be particular reasons where that ought to be done in a particular case, but it is not the normal practice, as long as what is being used is a document that has been the subject of disclosure as is required under the ordinary Rules so that material is not being introduced which is totally foreign to the normal scope of preparation of each party. The practical side, though, is that if the opposing side and if the Chamber are to follow effectively any extensive document based -- any extensive cross-examination based on a particular document such as a past statement or interview, we have seen in this trial, as in others, that it is much more useful to everybody if copies of that are available so that it can be followed as the cross-examination occurs. So that if any party is proposing to cross-examine on such a document or transcript, it would be, I would suggest, not only a courtesy but a step that would greatly facilitate the progress of the trial if there were copies available to be distributed either at the commencement of the cross-examination or at the commencement of cross-examination on that document. Now, I said those few words just to remind people of the general position and practice we have been following. Mr. Whiting, for reasons of caution but beyond that reasons which are not altogether clear to me even now, has specifically raised his possible use of this particular document, and that having been done, I can quite well understand Mr. Mansfield, Mr. Guy-Smith, and by his adoption of it Mr. Topolski keeping their options open over what it is that might be coming, and I think that's where we've got to at the moment. There's certainly nothing that's been advanced which would suggest to the Chamber that you might not cross-examine on this document if you thought it appropriate. When you do so, your particular line of cross-examination might lead to some further objection from your opponents or difficulty from the Chamber. That's just indicated out of caution, and we do suggest that if the questioning is going to be at all extensive to have a copy of the transcript of it available would be a practical step.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you for that guidance. I do have one inquiry which will help the Prosecution in the future with future witnesses, and that is: The Court stated that there's no problem with using a document, and I'm looking at page 23, "as long as what is being used is a document that has been the subject of disclosure as is required under the ordinary Rules." Now, as I understand that, and this is what's going to be helpful for us with respect to -- as the case continues, if I understand that, if a document was -- should have been disclosed under the Rules, whether it be 66(B) or 68, and it wasn't, then there may be a problem in using that document in cross-examination. However, if a document does not fall under those disclosure requirements, it is something completely separate, then we would not by virtue of using that document in cross-examination or intending to use it in cross-examination be required to disclose it until such time as we used in cross-examination. That's how I understand what the Court has said, but if I'm wrong --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There are ifs and buts about that. But if because of evidence in chief your attention has been directed in some new direction and in the course of that you come across a new document that is not a document that ought to have been specifically disclosed under any of the specific Rules but is a document that was in the general electronic material that is available to the other side, you wouldn't have any fundamental disclosure problem. You may have either from one of your opposing parties or all of them, or from the Bench, reason for delay if this took everybody by surprise before there was some re-examination on it. But -- understand that position?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I do. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Something that is totally unavailable to anybody before the moment you produce it, I would expect to hear a lot more from Mr. Mansfield and his colleagues. Now, have I gone too far away from where you'd like me to be, Mr. Mansfield?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: For the moment you're close enough. I several take up the offer of seeing what the transcript is. May I make two points only. One is we did a search of the EDS system -- I didn't do it myself, someone else did -- probably not long before the Prosecution did theirs, and certainly it takes many hours but those responsible for doing it did not turn this up. So the question may become in future to ensure that we know what it is that we're given notice so that we can check that it is on the system, because it may not have been disclosed at the point in which -- at the time in which we looked at the system. That's one practical problem. Can I just correct one thing that Mr. Whiting has said vis-a-vis the Defence reciprocation. He said we cross-examined a number of witnesses of whom there were interviews conducted by ourselves. We indicated that were we going to use those interviews in relation to Prosecution witnesses we would disclose the interview, and in fact on one occasion we did precisely that. We did give the Prosecution the interview. On the other occasions we didn't use them, and I think you may recall -- I think there's hardly any occasion I cross-examined on an interview with our own representatives. So we have tried to adopt that approach. I only make those two points. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, gentlemen. Now, Mr. Whiting, we've reached the point where you would have at most a quarter of an hour. Is that the most practical step forward or is an early break now more practical?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Either way. I'm happy to go either way. We can take the break now and I can disclose this document and week proceed. Or I can proceed now. I won't reach the document in the first 15 minutes. That's for certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have the witness brought back in, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: While the witness is being brought back in, what Mr. Mansfield said at the end there is absolutely correct. That position was made clear to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That took a little longer than a few moments, Mr. Selimi. I'm sorry for that. Now Mr. Whiting has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Selimi. My name is Alex Whiting. I'm one of the Prosecutors in this case. Can you understand me clearly?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I think I understood your testimony to say that you joined the KLA in 1994. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In 1996 you had to go to Prekaz?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall when that was in 1996?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In October.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that after 1996 when you went to Prekaz, after October 1996, that one of your tasks was to maintain contact with units in other regions of Kosovo? And when I say "units," I'm talking about KLA units.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. More or less, yes. It depends on what units I was familiar with at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, for example, units -- that were units in the Dukadjin zone that you were familiar with; correct?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In fact, you -- well, let me back up for a moment. In -- when you retreated to the -- or "retreat" is not the right word, but when you went to the -- to Prekaz in October of 1996, who else was there? Who did you associate with there in Prekaz?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met many comrades among whom Commander Adem Jashari and his co-fighters. If this is in your interest, I can cite some of the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, for example, you also met with Sylejman Selimi?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't need to meet him there because he's a very close member of my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. That was a badly phrased question. I mean is you saw him there. He was there also in Prekaz at that time?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at that time. He came there later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall when he came?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He used to come there often at night, but he too had to pass through a difficult situation as I did in October 1986. That was in January 1997 when Serbia launched a campaign of arrests, a time when he joined the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So if I understand your testimony, he -- he joined the KLA and came to -- and was in Prekaz after January of 1997?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I was unable to explain it right. He came to Prekaz. He used to come to Prekaz often because he didn't want to remain a civilian because he was being prosecuted until 1997. He had, in fact, joined the ranks of Adem Jashari's group since the 1990s, and he had joined the KLA from its formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you just tell us who some of the other people were, some of the other co-fighters in Adem Jashari's group, by sides yourself, Sylejman Selimi and Adem Jashari who are the other names?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hamze Jashari the brother of Adem Jashari. Sait Jashari. Muse Jashari, a cousin of his. A cousin of Adem Jashari. Fadil Kodra, a co-villager of Adem Jashari. Besim Rama, a co-villager of his. As well Nuredin Lushtaku, also a co-villager of Adem. And all of them were -- had joined the group of Adem Jashari. There were many others, but since you asked me to give you some names, they are some of the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Would you just give that last name again, Lushtaku? What was the first name, something Lushtaku.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nuredin Lushtaku.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, during -- during that time period and even earlier, were the KLA fighters who were based in Prekaz supplied with weapons by fighters in the Dukadjin zone? During 1995 and 1996.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may be so in some specific case, but not in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you have interactions at that time with Lahi Brahimi, Luan Haradinaj, Daut Haradinaj?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did you get weapons from them during 1996?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't get arms from them, but together with them we got arms in Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Didn't -- Lahi Brahimi lived in Jablanica; correct?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And he had -- he kept weapons at his house. That was one place where weapons were kept; correct?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And in fact, during 1995 and 1996, there wasn't much fighting in Dukadjin and so they could provide weapons to the fighters who were in the Drenica zone; correct?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't have so many weapons as to be able to give to others because there were other people there waiting to get weapons themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So your testimony is that you got the weapons from Albania with these people. You went with these people to Albania to get weapons?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: During 1996?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What was that? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: During 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: During 1997 you also went for training in Albania; correct?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You didn't go for two weeks of training in Golem in Albania?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was trained elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where were you trained?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Serbian police stations when they were maltreating me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several times. Since you referred to 1997, in 1997 too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you said that you went several times to Albania to get weapons during 1997. Can you be more specific? How many times?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I regret I cannot give you accurate dates. Maybe four, five, or six times, but I don't believe ten times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What kind of weapons did you bring back?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mainly infantry, light weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mortar shells?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what it is that you refer to as mortar shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You don't know what mortar shells are?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know it, of course, but there are two kinds of weapons which are described as mortars. What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You can educate me on that. What two types are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case, I believe you mean the rocket -- hand-held rocket launchers. This is what you mean, I suppose. But there are also mine launchers which are referred to as mortars by us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you -- in 1997, which of these kinds did you bring back?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first, the former. The hand-held rocket launchers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall going on one occasion to Albania with Daut Haradinaj, Kerim Kelmendi, Gzim Mehmeti [phoen], Sylejman Selimi, and you met up with Adrian Krasniqi and Ilir Konushevci?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow me to direct you your spelling, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You certainly can correct me on pronunciation, but then if you could answer the question.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Adem Krasniqi was not among them. It was Adrian Krasniqi. Yes, I went. This might have been in October 1997, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And with this group you didn't engage in training for two weeks while in Albania?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did others in your group engage in training?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They might have engaged in physical training in a special location, yes. This may have been so, because during that time I didn't stay with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where were you staying?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally stayed in Tirana, whereas they went to Golem.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you know that in fact they did engage in physical training in Golem for two weeks. You know that; right?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said they might have been engaged in physical exercises.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: My question is what you know. Do you know or not, or are you just speculating?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not speculating, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you return to Kosovo with this group?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you return to Kosovo on your own?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't return on my own. I returned after two or three days. I returned on the 16th of October [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And who was with you when you returned?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Haki Hajdari might have been the person who was with me. He was from Drenica. But for the moment it escaped me who was the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps this is a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will have now the first break and resume at five minutes after four o'clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Selimi, did you engage in fighting in around November 1997 in Acereva? And I'm sure I mispronounced that incorrectly [sic] as well but I think you know what I mean. Did you understand the question? Did you engage in fighting there?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. Just wait a moment. Your microphone has to be turned on. Now, if you could answer the question.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning I would like to make a correction because I see something different regarding a date in the transcript. It's in the first page of the transcript. It's not how I said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What's the correction?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here it says that I returned from Albania on the 16th of October. What I said is that I returned from Albania after the 16th of October. Maybe this is not of great relevance, but just for me to correct it. Now I will proceed with my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall -- do you want me to repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was involved in most of the events dealing with KLA in Drenica in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did that include a battle at Acereva?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't call it a battle, but it did include Acereva, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, wasn't there fighting that lasted for some hours with -- and it was between the -- between KLA soldiers and the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were fightings, but the fighting was going on at Ludoviq village, which is not far from Acereva.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And both of those villages are close to Likovc; correct?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not very close if we take into consideration the distance between Ludoviq and Acereva. Likovc is on their south, maybe ten kilometres from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. And the Serb forces came. They had a helicopter, armoured vehicles, a tank. You're nodding your head yes, but you have to answer audibly or it won't be picked up on the transcript. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And how long did that fighting last, for a number of hours?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fighting began at 9.15 and continued for several hours until noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What was the result of the fighting?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We gained victory. The Serb forces had withdrawn, and they suffered casualties both in military technique and in manpower. We didn't have any injured amongst us. During their withdrawal, the Serb forces retaliated on the population, and in this event they shot at a teacher.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That was Halit Geci; is that right?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was Halit Geci.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This battle was in November, late November 1997?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 26th of November, 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You went to the funeral for Halit Geci?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And in fact, that was an important event because two of you -- one or two of you did not -- I think two of you did not wear masks, correct, or took off your masks?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was important.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I believe you testified in response to my first question about this subject that you were involved in all the fightings in Drenica that occurred at this time period. Did I recall your testimony correctly?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I recall my answer, and I will repeat it. Almost in all the fightings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Focusing on 1996 and 1997, can you tell the Court what kind of fighting you engaged in? Describe generally. What are you talking about, all the fighting?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to be helpful. During 1996, the Kosovo Liberation Army undertook several actions or attacks on Serb police stations, and I participated in one of these actions. In addition, in 1997 it was more or less the same but of more or less greater intensity. I participated in other actions as well, actions against the Serb police stationed in their police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The action that you referred to in 1996 against the Serb police station, where was that?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the Serb police station in Kliqine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: May municipality is that in?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is nearby the main road that links Klina and Peja. I think it is in Peja municipality. Nonetheless, it can be in Klina municipality as well, but it's on the border between Klina and Peja municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said that you attacked a police station. Can you just describe for us how you attacked the police station?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: With a shell called tromblon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know what the result of the attack was?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't know exactly what the result was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, do you know if anybody was injured?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Aside from that action, did you participate in any other actions, military actions, during 1996?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think no, not actions of this nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Actions of any other nature?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The year of 1996 was very important as for the organisation and development of the KLA. I was focused in the development of this structure, and my entire activity at that time is linked with this. In 1996 was also important for me personally because at that time the indictment of the Serbian police against me was made public, and I could now pass into another form of activity which was at that time called activity in flee, exile.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: During 1997, you said that you engaged in other actions against the Serb police. What other kinds of actions did you engage in during that year, 1997?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was an action, a coordinated one, between the KLA units which operated at that time, and this was exclusively targeting police stations in the area of Kosova. I call it a synchronised action because the actions were carried out in different locations in Kosova. I participated in such an action against the Serb police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I launched a hand-held rocket launcher shell to the -- against the police station in Rakovc.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What other police stations were targeted?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to remember some of the police stations. In Decan, Irzniq, Celopek, Klina, Kijeve, Drenas, and so on. I have the impression that at that time 12 police station were is attacked in the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember when in 1997 that happened?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: On 11th of November at 11.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: During 1997 did you engage in any other actions on behalf of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What were they?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was ambushed twice at Serb police checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What do you mean you were ambushed?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I moved a lot, moved to designated places in Drenica and Dukadjin, and while moving from one place to another there were a lot of Serb police checkpoints, and I fell into their ambush. But, however, I did move continuously.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did that -- when you say you fell into their ambush, did that result in fighting or were you just detained?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We exchanged fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That occurred on two occasions in 1997?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember when and where?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time was in the city of Drenas, former Gllogovc, and secondly in Klina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you -- in 1997, aside from the attack on the police station in Rakovc and these two ambushes you have described, did you participate in any other actions on behalf of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the impression that even these that I mentioned were not a few, but no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when you say -- when I say "actions," you understand I mean any kind of violent attack, any kind of military attack on -- of any kind?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know what you mean, but my answer is no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you ever -- you yourself -- I'll ask the question about you yourself first. Did you yourself ever target Serb civilians during 1996 and 1997?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was not our goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you certain about that, Mr. Selimi?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did that ever change, for example in 1998 or 1999?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did the KLA, to your knowledge, ever arrest or detain Serb civilians?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you call arrest or detention, because the KLA did not have prisons for it to have detentions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did the KLA ever, during the war, 1998, 1999, did the KLA ever have a facility that it used to detain people? And when I say "facility," I mean a house, a building, anything.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had facilities which were not enough for our own soldiers. All the houses of people in the areas of responsibility were shared with the soldiers. Nonetheless, they were not enough for the soldiers, for them to shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Selimi, I don't think you answered my question. My question was: Did the KLA ever, during the war -- I'll make it more broad. 1997, 1998, 1999, did the KLA ever, to your knowledge, have a building -- house, building that it used to detain people?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, and it didn't have. I'm saying I don't know because nobody ever informed me about that, and I'm saying it didn't have because personally I didn't see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you never heard about people being detained during those years by the KLA. Never heard about a single person being detained by the KLA during 1997, 1998, 1999.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said was that I didn't see any. As for hearing, if you refer to propaganda, that's another issue. But I didn't have knowledge for the existence of such a facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you mention "propaganda," what are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two sorts of propaganda regarding the KLA warfare. One launched bit Serb forces in order to accuse the KLA; and on the other side the KLA propaganda, the propaganda that it applied for certain reasons and which served for mobilising people. So both parties had their own propaganda.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And so your testimony is putting aside propaganda, and I assume you're talking in this respect about Serb propaganda, you never heard about anybody being detained by the KLA during 1997, 1998, 1999? Is that a fair summary of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There might have been detentions, but not prisons. I don't know of any specific or particular case that has stuck in my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And I take it when you say there might have been detentions, you're talking there about brief detentions?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Because a detention that -- of more than a day or two would require something -- some kind of a prison; correct? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not refer to one day or two days. What I mean by small amount of time, that is what you need to verify somebody's identity. If there is a need to speculate, then we can speculate, but as I said, I don't remember any particular case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I don't want you to speculate, Mr. Selimi, but as I understood -- just so I'm clear on your testimony, you don't remember yourself any instances even of a brief detention?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I might recall, but I do not recall names because this was no -- it was not my preoccupation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you do recall?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since there were checkpoints on certain locations and roads, these checkpoints were created to stop people that were passing by and not helicopters, and people were stopped at these checkpoints until we verified their identities and until we were sure, and then they were released to go to their destinations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How long would they be stopped at the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: From one minute to several hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But your testimony is no more than several hours?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Selimi, I put the question about you originally, but I'm going to put it more broadly. Are you aware of the KLA, during 1996, 1997, 1998 ever targeting Serb civilians in a military action or a violent action, ever targeting Serb civilians? You said you never did it. Are you aware of the KLA ever doing it?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Selimi, you're aware that at least by 1997 the KLA had a policy expressed through communiques of targeting people suspected of collaborating with the Serbs. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You don't remember at any time a policy of the KLA of targeting people suspected of collaborating?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to be clear. Do you mean if there was such a policy, or are you saying that you heard it in the communiques? I want to know what you're referring to, to the communiques or to the policy again the collaborators? I will try to be helpful as much as I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Selimi, it's you testifying, not me. So the question is what you know about a policy of the KLA that -- targeting collaborators. Are you aware of that policy?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we look at the aim and the struggle waged by the KLA, its objective was to attack the main institutions, the main mechanisms -- three main mechanisms of the state power, direct mechanisms that used systematic violence against the Albanian people of Kosovo, namely the police, the army, and the secret service or intelligence service.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You didn't answer my question, Mr. Selimi. The question was: Were you aware of a policy by the KLA to target people suspected of collaborating, Albanians suspected of collaborating with the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise for not answering you completely, but I'll try to answer your question again. The target of the struggle of the KLA was, I want to specify, the system of -- intelligence system of Serbia which exerted violence on the Albanians. Within this system there may be and certainly there were Albanians involved in it. Not as suspects, but since they were involved they were part of the system. They were and should be the target of the attacks by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, would you agree with this definition of a collaborator? You have said persons involved with the system. Let me put a definition to you and see if you agree with it. "A collaborator is a person who causes the country damage, a person harmful to the KLA when such a person is giving information on the movements of the KLA to the Belgrade regime." Is that a definition of collaborator that you would agree with?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that would be all, but generally since we have to agree on a definition, yes. All the collaborators of the Serb secret service were not those who provided information on the positions of the KLA but those people and those individuals involved in the structures of the intelligence service called the Serbian secret service or the UDB. There may be people who might have been forced to provide information to Serbia about the positions of the KLA, something that has happened not rarely, but these people are not to blame.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So your testimony is that you would not include as a collaborator some people who gave information or who were too close to the Serb authorities? You would not include those people in your definition of collaborator?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They cannot be called collaborators.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because most of them have supplied information under pressure, under use of force to the Serbian secret service. Anyone who'd fall in the hands of the Serbs would certainly give information on the KLA and its positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So in your view it would be improper to target somebody in that category; correct?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Collaborators, in your view, should be limited only to people who are actually working for the police?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The collaborators are those people who were part of the repressive Serb regime. In this case, part of the secret -- state secret service.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In what way part of the state secret service? What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the most dangerous mechanisms of Serbia used against the Albanians was the UDB, the state secret service supported by the police. Since this service and this structure, this repressive structure exerted violence against the Albanians, everyone who was involved in this structure was a tool of Serb repression against the Albanians, and we considered them equal to the Serb police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what do you mean "involved in the structure"? Do you mean actually employed by the secret police or by the police or army, or do you mean something more?

utterances.speaker: REXHEP SELIMI [Resumed]
